name: Argob
title: Figure mentioned in connection with Pekah's coup against King Pekahiah
summary: Argob appears in 2 Kings 15:25 in connection with Pekah's coup against King Pekahiah of Israel in the fortress at Samaria. His exact role is a subject of considerable debate among scholars: he may have been a royal official who was killed along with Pekahiah, or one of Pekah's co-conspirators. The uncertainty is heightened by the fact that the Septuagint completely omits both Argob and Arje from the verse, leading several textual critics to regard the names as secondary additions in the Hebrew text. In addition, it has been suggested that 'Argob' may originally have been a geographical reference to the region of Argob in Bashan, which through scribal tradition became misplaced in the account of the coup. Argob thus remains one of the most enigmatic names in the Books of Kings.

keyEvents.title: Pekah's Coup Against King Pekahiah in Samaria
keyEvents.description: Pekah, son of Remaliah, led a conspiracy against King Pekahiah of Israel and killed him in the fortress within the royal palace at Samaria, with support from 50 Gileadites. Argob and Arje are mentioned in this context, but it is debated whether they were victims of the coup or co-conspirators.

keyEvents.title: Pekah's Seizure of Power After the Coup
keyEvents.description: After the murder of Pekahiah, Pekah took the throne as king over Israel. Whether Argob survived the coup or was killed along with Pekahiah is not clearly stated in the text.

versions.summary: Argob is a person mentioned in 2 Kings 15:25 in connection with the murder of King Pekahiah of Israel. He was likely an official or military leader at the court in Samaria. His exact role in the conspiracy is debated among biblical scholars.

His exact role in the event is disputed: it is unclear whether he was a royal official who was killed along with Pekahiah, or one of the conspirators who supported Pekah. Textual uncertainty is reinforced by the fact that the Septuagint omits both Argob and Arje from the verse. Several scholars have also suggested that 'Argob' may originally have been a place name (the region of Argob in Bashan) which, due to a scribal error, was incorporated into the account of the coup.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew text in 2 Kings 15:25 mentions Argob and Arje together with Pekah and 50 Gileadites. However, the Greek translation (Septuagint) omits the names Argob and Arje entirely, leading several textual critics to regard them as a later addition (gloss) in the Hebrew text.

The name 'Argob' also appears as a place name—a region in Bashan (Deut 3:4, 13–14; 1 Kings 4:13). Some scholars have suggested that the mention in 2 Kings 15:25 was originally a geographical reference that, due to a scribal error, ended up in the wrong context, possibly from verse 29 which describes Tiglath-Pileser's conquests in the region.

The period around 740–730 BC in the northern kingdom of Israel was marked by extreme political instability. From the death of Jeroboam II to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, four out of six kings were murdered by their successors, reflecting the deep crisis in the northern kingdom as it faced the expanding Neo-Assyrian Empire.

The Gileadites who participated in Pekah's coup may be linked to tensions between the Transjordan tribes and the central court in Samaria. Pekah himself appears to have had his power base in Gilead, giving the coup a regional political dimension.

The Hebrew name 'Argob' (אַרְגֹּב) may possibly relate to the root r-g-b, which is associated with 'clod of earth' or 'heap of stones.' As a place name, it denoted a fertile but stony area in Bashan. This dual use of the name as both a personal and geographical designation contributes to the ongoing interpretive debate.
